Clickbait, here understood as content designed to attract attention and encourage clicks through misleading or sensationalized headlines at the expense of informativeness (Potthast et al., 2016), has become a widely studied phenomenon in news and social media research. The prevalence of such content across major platforms has motivated a substantial body of detection work, ranging from simple lexical classifiers to transformer-based models. Our work contributes to this line of research by focusing on a neglected subtype: clickbait that is factually accurate but emotionally manipulative.

Stance detection — the task of inferring an author's position toward a given target from text (Mohammad et al., 2016) — has received sustained attention in NLP, with applications ranging from political discourse analysis to rumor verification. The task differs from sentiment analysis in an important respect: a document may be uniformly positive in tone while expressing opposition to the stated target. This asymmetry between affect and stance motivates the use of argument structure features that go beyond surface polarity signals. Several multilingual datasets have been introduced in recent years, though coverage of morphologically rich and low-resource languages remains sparse.

We focus on clinical notes containing descriptions of adverse drug events (ADEs), defined as any harmful or unintended response to a medication administered at a standard dose (Edwards and Aronson, 2000). ADE detection in free-text clinical documentation presents unique challenges relative to structured reporting systems: events are frequently described in hedged or speculative language, and relevant information is often distributed across multiple sentences or even visits. Our pipeline addresses both challenges through a combination of negation resolution and cross-sentence aggregation.

The concept of algorithmic accountability has emerged as a focal point in debates about the governance of automated decision-making systems in high-stakes domains such as criminal justice, lending, and hiring. While accountability is sometimes used loosely to mean any form of oversight or transparency, we follow Bovens (2007) in treating it as a specific social relationship in which an actor is obligated to explain and justify its conduct to a forum, which can impose consequences for unsatisfactory explanations. This narrower definition is important because it distinguishes accountability from mere explainability: a system can be explainable without being accountable if there is no forum empowered to sanction it. Our annotation scheme for court opinions is designed around this distinction, separating passages that invoke explanatory language from those that assign enforceable responsibilities. The practical stakes of this distinction are illustrated by several high-profile cases in which detailed audit reports failed to produce meaningful remediation.

Emotional granularity — the degree to which individuals make fine-grained distinctions among their emotional experiences rather than collapsing them into broad valence categories (Barrett et al., 2001) — has been linked to a range of health and social outcomes, including emotion regulation capacity and interpersonal functioning. Computational proxies for granularity based on the distribution of emotion vocabulary in personal writing have been proposed as a low-cost alternative to experience sampling methods. Our work evaluates the validity of these proxies against diary-based ground truth in a sample of undergraduate participants.

We annotate each sentence pair in our dataset for the presence of discourse coherence relations following the Penn Discourse Treebank taxonomy (Prasad et al., 2008). Relations such as Contrast, Elaboration, and Cause are marked at the implicit and explicit level, with implicit relations — those inferred without a lexical connective — treated as a separate annotation tier. Our inter-annotator agreement analysis reports Cohen's kappa separately for explicit and implicit relations, as the two have consistently different agreement profiles in prior annotation studies.

Throughout this paper, we use the term microaggression to refer to brief, commonplace verbal or behavioral indignities — whether intentional or unintentional — that communicate denigrating messages to members of marginalized groups (Sue et al., 2007). This encompasses both overtly hostile acts and subtler forms of exclusion that may not be recognized as harmful by their perpetrators. The challenge for automated detection is precisely this subtlety: unlike hate speech or explicit slurs, microaggressions depend heavily on context, identity, and the relationship between interlocutors, making surface-level pattern matching insufficient. Our detection system addresses this through a combination of pragmatic inference and social context encoding.

Data-to-text generation — the task of producing natural language descriptions from structured records such as database tables, knowledge graphs, or sports statistics (Gatt and Krahmer, 2018) — has seen a surge of interest following the release of large neural sequence-to-sequence models. The core challenge lies in faithfully grounding generated text in the input records while producing fluent and varied output. Recent work has examined this tension primarily in single-domain settings; we extend the evaluation to a cross-domain benchmark.

Vaccine hesitancy — a delay in acceptance or refusal of vaccines despite availability of vaccination services (MacDonald et al., 2015) — exists on a spectrum. At one end are individuals with mild reservations who may be persuaded by clear information; at the other are committed opponents whose positions are unlikely to change regardless of evidence. Treating these groups as a monolithic category has been cited as a failure mode in public health communication, leading to interventions that are either too gentle for the committed and too confrontational for the hesitant. Our computational work contributes to this problem by developing a continuous scoring model for hesitancy severity from social media text, rather than performing binary classification. We draw on a corpus of vaccination-related posts across five platforms, spanning both pro- and anti-vaccination communities.

Following Toulmin (1958), we distinguish six functional components of an argument: claim, data, warrant, backing, qualifier, and rebuttal. This decomposition has become a standard reference point in argument mining, though individual annotation projects have adopted varying subsets depending on the genre and level of detail required. Our annotation guidelines use the full six-component scheme but collapse qualifier and rebuttal into a single hedging category for practical reasons, given their low frequency in our corpus of online news comments. Annotators were trained on a set of worked examples before independently labeling a calibration batch.

Alternative splicing, the process by which a single gene can produce multiple distinct mRNA transcripts through differential inclusion of exonic segments (Blencowe, 2006), is estimated to affect the majority of multi-exon genes in the human genome. Predicting which isoforms are expressed in specific tissue types from sequence features alone remains an open problem. We approach this as a sequence classification task, encoding exon-intron boundaries as binary features in a sliding window around each splice site.

Polarization in political discourse has been operationalized in a variety of ways in both political science and computational research: ideological distance between party medians, affective hostility toward the outgroup, and the collapse of cross-cutting cleavages, among others. We follow Iyengar et al. (2019) in distinguishing ideological polarization — divergence in policy positions — from affective polarization, which refers to the degree of dislike and distrust that members of one party hold toward the opposing party, irrespective of substantive policy disagreements. This distinction has important consequences for measurement: affective polarization can increase even when policy positions remain stable. Our corpus analysis targets affective polarization as the primary construct, using language-based proxies for intergroup hostility derived from survey validation studies.

We define dog whistles — political messaging that carries an overt, innocuous meaning for general audiences while simultaneously signaling a covert, often discriminatory meaning to a targeted subgroup (Henderson and McCready, 2019) — as our primary annotation target. Dog whistles are particularly challenging for automated systems because their harmful content is deliberately obscured: classifiers trained on surface hate speech features will systematically miss them. Our annotation protocol requires raters to consider both the surface-level message and the plausible interpretations available to different audience communities.

Metacognition — the capacity to monitor and regulate one's own cognitive processes (Flavell, 1979) — has long been identified as a key predictor of academic success and transfer of learning. Despite this, automated approaches to assessing metacognitive activity in student writing remain limited, with most work focusing on surface linguistic markers rather than the underlying reasoning processes. We contribute a dataset of annotated think-aloud protocols with fine-grained metacognitive labels.

Bridging anaphora — the phenomenon in which an anaphor refers to an entity not previously mentioned explicitly, but inferrable from another entity in the discourse (Clark, 1975) — has received comparatively little attention in coreference resolution, with most systems and benchmarks focusing on identity coreference. This neglect is significant: bridging expressions are common in naturally occurring text and their resolution requires world knowledge and pragmatic inference that identity-coreference models are not equipped to provide. Several annotated resources have been developed in recent years, covering newswire and Wikipedia, though narrative fiction remains underexplored.

Cyberbullying has been defined variously across disciplines, creating challenges for cross-study comparison and automated detection. For the purposes of this work, we adopt the definition from Hinduja and Patchin (2014), who characterize it as willful and repeated harm inflicted through the use of computers, cell phones, and other electronic devices. This definition emphasizes two features — repetition and intent — that are particularly relevant for classification: a single aggressive message may not constitute cyberbullying even if it is severe, and unintentional harm falls outside the scope. Our labeling guidelines instruct annotators to apply these criteria, marking only exchanges that show evidence of recurrence and deliberate targeting. This is one of several definitional choices that distinguish our dataset from prior resources in the area.

Extreme summarization — the task of producing a single-sentence summary capturing the core argument of a news article rather than a multi-sentence abstract (Narayan et al., 2018) — demands more aggressive content selection than standard summarization benchmarks. This makes it a useful testbed for models that must prioritize rather than compress. We evaluate our approach on the XSum dataset introduced by Narayan et al., which remains the standard benchmark for this variant of the task.

The notion of fairness invoked in this paper is group fairness in the sense of demographic parity: the requirement that a classifier's outputs be statistically independent of membership in a protected group (Dwork et al., 2012). We acknowledge that this is one of several competing formalizations in the literature — counterfactual fairness, equalized odds, and calibration within groups have each been advocated by different communities — and that these definitions are in general mathematically incompatible. The choice to adopt demographic parity as our primary criterion is driven by the regulatory context of our application domain, in which equal outcome rates across demographic groups constitute the legally operationalized standard.

Embodied cognition — the view that cognitive processes are grounded in sensorimotor experience rather than abstract symbolic manipulation (Barsalou, 1999) — has implications for how language models should be expected to represent meaning. A model trained exclusively on text lacks access to the perceptual grounding that this view holds to be constitutive of conceptual content. We examine whether vision-language models show patterns of concept representation more consistent with this view than text-only models.

Our dataset consists of judicial opinions in which courts adjudicate claims of disparate impact discrimination. Disparate impact, as established in Griggs v. Duke Power Co. and subsequently formalized in employment law scholarship, refers to facially neutral policies or practices that have a disproportionately adverse effect on members of a protected class, regardless of discriminatory intent (Rutherglen, 1987). This is distinct from disparate treatment, which requires proof of intentional discrimination. The distinction matters for our annotation task: passages invoking impact-based reasoning often lack the explicit intent language that characterizes treatment-based claims, making them harder to identify through surface-level pattern matching. Annotators were provided with worked examples of both types before labeling.

We address the task of machine reading comprehension (MRC), broadly defined as the ability to extract or infer answers to natural language questions from a given passage or document collection (Hirschman et al., 1999). The field has evolved substantially from early template-filling approaches to the current landscape of span extraction and generative QA models. Our focus is on a specific failure mode in MRC systems: their tendency to exploit statistical shortcuts in question-passage pairs rather than performing genuine textual reasoning, a problem that has motivated the development of adversarial and contrast datasets in recent years.

Homophily — the tendency for individuals to associate with others who are similar to them in socially relevant attributes (McPherson et al., 2001) — is one of the most robust empirical regularities in social network analysis. Its presence in online communities has implications for the spread of information, norms, and misinformation, as well as for the effectiveness of cross-group bridging interventions. We quantify homophily along both ideological and linguistic dimensions in a large Reddit corpus.

In this work, we target discontinuous constituency structures — parse trees in which the yield of a non-terminal node is not a contiguous substring of the input sentence (Maier, 2010). Such structures arise frequently in free word-order languages and in constructions such as extraposition, topicalization, and heavy NP shift in English. Handling them requires extensions to standard chart-parsing algorithms, and most widely used parsers either ignore them or recover them via post-processing heuristics. We propose an end-to-end model that handles discontinuities natively within a span-based parsing framework.

Alexithymia — a personality trait characterized by difficulty identifying and describing one's own emotional states, limited imaginative capacity, and an externally oriented cognitive style (Sifneos, 1973) — has been linked to a range of adverse outcomes including increased risk of somatic disorders, impaired social functioning, and reduced response to psychotherapy. Despite its clinical relevance, assessment relies almost exclusively on self-report questionnaires, which are susceptible to the very introspective limitations the construct describes. Computational approaches to inferring alexithymia from natural language are nascent but promising, with preliminary evidence that the construct leaves detectable traces in emotional vocabulary diversity, first-person emotional language frequency, and response patterns in clinical interviews. Our work advances this line by training and evaluating a model on therapist-rated alexithymia scores from a longitudinal outpatient sample.

We annotate each dialogue turn with a dialogue act label following the ISO 24617-2 standard (Bunt et al., 2012), which defines dialogue acts as communicative functions that a speaker performs through an utterance, such as informing, questioning, or accepting. This functional annotation layer is used to train an auxiliary classifier whose outputs are concatenated with the semantic representations at inference time.

Racial gaslighting — the practice of causing members of a marginalized racial group to question the validity of their experiences of discrimination (Davis and Ernst, 2019) — presents particular challenges for content moderation systems. Unlike overt hate speech, racial gaslighting operates through denial, minimization, and appeals to colorblindness, making it difficult to identify without contextual information about the interaction. Our annotation study focuses on this construct in the context of responses to first-person accounts of discrimination posted on Reddit.

Implicit bias in text classification refers to systematic patterns in model behavior that disadvantage particular groups without explicit discriminatory inputs — arising instead from statistical regularities in training data (Shah et al., 2020). This is distinct from dataset bias, which concerns the composition of the training corpus itself, and from model bias, which concerns architectural inductive biases. The three often interact, but conflating them impedes targeted mitigation: a solution appropriate for dataset imbalance may be ineffective or counterproductive for implicit behavioral bias. We use Shah et al.'s (2020) tripartite framing throughout this paper to organize our analysis of bias sources and mitigation strategies in toxicity classification systems.

Abductive reasoning — inferring the most plausible explanation for an observed set of facts (Josephson and Josephson, 1994) — has attracted growing interest in NLP as a capability distinct from deductive and inductive reasoning. Unlike deduction, abduction produces defeasible conclusions that may be revised in light of new evidence. We contribute a diagnostic suite targeting abductive reasoning specifically in multi-document contexts, where the evidence for a hypothesis is distributed across several passages.

Our corpus consists of filings submitted to the Securities and Exchange Commission under Regulation FD, which governs the disclosure of material non-public information. Materiality — the standard that determines whether information must be disclosed — is defined in securities law as information that a reasonable investor would consider significant in making an investment decision (Hazen, 2009). This definition is intentionally flexible, and its application to specific disclosures is often contested. Our annotation task asks legal experts to identify sentences in 8-K filings that describe potentially material events, using this standard as the guiding criterion.

The term low-resource is used with considerable variation in the NLP literature, sometimes referring to the absence of large annotated training sets, sometimes to limited digitized text of any kind, and sometimes to the combination of both. For clarity, we follow Cieri et al. (2016) in defining a language as low-resource for a given task when the available labeled training data falls below the minimum threshold at which standard supervised approaches achieve acceptable performance on that task. This task-relative definition is preferable to a fixed token threshold because data requirements vary substantially across tasks: named entity recognition may be tractable with a few hundred examples, while machine translation typically requires orders of magnitude more. Throughout this paper, we report results for languages meeting this criterion for part-of-speech tagging specifically, with the threshold determined by the learning curve analysis in Section 4.

Irony, in the sense adopted here, involves a speaker meaning the opposite or near-opposite of what is literally expressed, typically for rhetorical or humorous effect (Grice, 1975). Automated irony detection has proven particularly resistant to progress, as the cues that signal ironic intent — prosody, shared knowledge, contextual incongruity — are difficult to encode in text-only systems. We examine whether cross-lingual transfer can provide indirect access to some of these cues through shared pragmatic patterns.

We restrict our dataset to posts exhibiting signs of acute psychological distress, operationalized following the concept of a mental health crisis as a period in which a person's normal coping strategies are overwhelmed and immediate risk of harm to self or others is elevated (Caplan, 1964). This is a stricter criterion than general mental health disclosure, and it is reflected in our sampling strategy: we focus on posts from dedicated crisis forums and threads flagged by moderators for urgent attention. Posts expressing general sadness or chronic mental health challenges without acute risk indicators are excluded.

Translation quality is a multidimensional concept that resists reduction to a single score or ranking. Human translators and professional evaluators typically distinguish at minimum between adequacy — the degree to which the translation conveys the meaning of the source — and fluency — the degree to which it reads as natural text in the target language (White et al., 1994). These two dimensions are not redundant: a translation can be highly adequate but stilted, or fluent but unfaithful. Our evaluation framework reports both dimensions separately, using a direct assessment protocol for adequacy and a fluency rating task administered to native speakers of the target language with no knowledge of the source. We also report a composite score for convenience but treat it as a secondary measure.

We define brigading — coordinated mass reporting or negative engagement targeting a specific user or post, typically organized outside the platform itself (Mariconti et al., 2019) — as the phenomenon of interest in this study. Detecting brigading in real time is a content moderation priority for major platforms, but the covert organization that precedes it makes it difficult to distinguish from organic spikes in engagement. Our detection model uses network coordination signals alongside linguistic features to identify likely brigading events.

Semantic transparency — the extent to which the meaning of a complex word or phrase is predictable from the meanings of its constituents (Libben, 1998) — is a key variable in morphological processing research. Compound words such as 'blackbird' and 'bluebell' occupy opposite ends of the transparency spectrum: the former's meaning is not inferrable from its parts, while the latter's is, at least partially. This variation has implications for automated morphological analysis, as opaque compounds require lexical lookup strategies that transparent ones do not. We incorporate a transparency score as a feature in our compound splitting model, estimated from distributional similarity between the compound and its constituent words.

Semantic role labeling (SRL) — the task of identifying, for each predicate in a sentence, the arguments that participate in the described event and the semantic roles they bear (Palmer et al., 2005) — has been central to NLP research for two decades, with applications spanning question answering, information extraction, and machine translation. Standard SRL annotations follow PropBank or FrameNet conventions, each reflecting different theories of predicate-argument structure. Recent neural approaches have achieved strong performance on standard benchmarks but exhibit marked degradation on out-of-domain text, particularly in specialized domains where predicates bear non-prototypical argument structures. Our work focuses on this domain generalization problem, introducing a cross-domain evaluation suite that spans five genres.

Proportionality — the principle that the burdens imposed by a legal measure must bear a reasonable relationship to the objectives it serves (Barak, 2012) — functions as a central organizing concept in constitutional adjudication across many jurisdictions. Despite its prominence in legal reasoning, computational work on proportionality review remains limited, in part because the reasoning it involves is deeply contextual and resistant to formalization. We present an annotated corpus of European Court of Human Rights judgments with proportionality reasoning spans marked.

Ontological commitment — the set of entities, properties, and relations that a representation system presupposes to exist (Gruber, 1993) — varies substantially across knowledge graph schemas, making cross-KG integration a non-trivial alignment problem. Our work targets this alignment problem specifically in the biomedical domain, where multiple KGs representing overlapping biological phenomena have been developed independently by different communities with different ontological commitments. We frame KG alignment as a structured prediction task, training on manually curated entity and relation mappings across three source KGs.

Natural language inference (NLI) — the task of determining whether a hypothesis sentence is entailed by, contradicts, or is neutral with respect to a premise sentence (Dagan et al., 2006) — has become one of the most widely used benchmarks for evaluating the semantic understanding capabilities of language models. The task abstracts over a range of reasoning phenomena including lexical entailment, logical reasoning, and world knowledge, making it a useful proxy for general language understanding. Performance on NLI has improved dramatically with the introduction of large pre-trained models, though recent work has shown that high NLI accuracy can be achieved through dataset artifacts rather than genuine reasoning.

Our work targets sycophancy in large language models, by which we mean the tendency of a model to produce responses that align with a user's expressed or implied preferences regardless of their accuracy (Sharma et al., 2023). This is distinct from politeness or stylistic accommodation: a sycophantic model may agree with factually incorrect statements, reverse correct positions when challenged, or selectively present information to confirm a user's prior beliefs. The phenomenon poses particular risks in high-stakes advisory contexts where users may be seeking genuine expert judgment rather than validation.

Deception detection research has grappled with the definitional question of what constitutes a lie. We follow Mahon (2016) in adopting a narrow definition: a lie is an assertion that the speaker believes to be false and intends the listener to believe. This excludes performative assertions, irony, and brainstorming — cases where the speaker's communicative intent is understood by both parties not to involve a sincere truth claim. The narrowness of this definition is intentional: broader definitions that include misleading true statements or paltering are better treated as distinct phenomena requiring separate modeling approaches.

Knowledge distillation refers to the process of training a smaller student model to reproduce the output distribution of a larger teacher model, rather than training directly on hard labels (Hinton et al., 2015). The core insight is that the soft probability distributions produced by a large model over incorrect classes carry information about the model's learned representations — information that is discarded when training on one-hot labels. This technique has become a standard component of model compression pipelines and has been applied across virtually every NLP task. Our work evaluates distillation under distribution shift, asking whether the implicit knowledge transferred from teacher to student is robust to domain changes at inference time.

Throughout this work we use the term counterfactual fairness to refer to the criterion that a model's prediction for an individual should be the same in the actual world and in any counterfactual world in which the individual's protected attributes differ but all causally downstream variables are adjusted accordingly (Kusner et al., 2017). This causal framing distinguishes counterfactual fairness from purely statistical criteria such as demographic parity or equalized odds, and it requires an explicit causal model of the relationships among features, protected attributes, and outcomes. We construct such a causal model from domain knowledge for our hiring outcome prediction setting before evaluating our classifier against this criterion.

Epistemic injustice, in the sense developed by Fricker (2007), refers to wrongs done to individuals specifically in their capacity as knowers — either through undermining their credibility as informants (testimonial injustice) or through a lack of conceptual resources to make sense of their experience (hermeneutical injustice). The concept has gained traction in AI ethics discussions as a framework for understanding how automated systems can harm users not just materially but epistemically, by dismissing or misclassifying their communications. Our annotation study examines whether NLP systems exhibit systematic patterns consistent with testimonial injustice across speakers of different demographic backgrounds.

Zero-shot learning in NLP refers to the ability of a model to perform a task or generalize to a class of examples it has not encountered during training, relying instead on semantic descriptions, attributes, or relationships to the training distribution (Xian et al., 2018). The distinction between zero-shot and few-shot generalization has become increasingly important as large language models are evaluated on their ability to follow novel instructions, with zero-shot evaluation providing a stricter test of whether a model's capabilities are truly general or depend on in-context demonstrations. Our evaluation protocol strictly separates zero-shot and few-shot conditions across all tasks.

Narrative transportation — the experience of being absorbed into a story world to the point where real-world concerns recede from awareness (Green and Brock, 2000) — has been studied as a mechanism by which fiction influences readers' beliefs and attitudes. High transportation is associated with reduced counterarguing and increased acceptance of narrative-consistent beliefs, even when those beliefs are factually incorrect. Our work examines whether language model-generated stories elicit transportation responses comparable to human-authored stories, using a validated transportation scale administered after reading.

We focus on what the literature calls pragmatic presuppositions — background assumptions that a speaker takes for granted as already accepted by the listener, and which are not the main point of the assertion (Levinson, 1983). Unlike conversational implicatures, presuppositions project under negation and other operators: both 'John stopped smoking' and 'John didn't stop smoking' presuppose that John used to smoke. This projection behavior is what makes presupposition particularly relevant for the analysis of loaded political language, where harmful or misleading content is often communicated via presupposed rather than asserted content.

Social determinants of health refer to the non-medical factors that influence health outcomes — including economic stability, educational attainment, neighborhood environment, and social relationships (Marmot and Wilkinson, 2005). These factors are documented to a highly variable degree in clinical text: some, such as housing instability, are routinely noted when they prompt clinical action, while others, such as chronic stress, are rarely mentioned even when clinically relevant. Our information extraction system targets this documentation gap, identifying mentions of all five SDOH categories in discharge summaries.

Deliberative democracy theory holds that political legitimacy derives not merely from aggregating preferences through voting but from the quality of the reasoning process by which citizens arrive at those preferences (Habermas, 1984; Cohen, 1989). Online discussion platforms have been examined as potential spaces for deliberative exchange, though empirical assessments have generally found that actual discourse falls short of deliberative ideals along multiple dimensions. Cohen (1989) articulates the criteria that genuine deliberation must satisfy — including inclusion, reasoning from public rather than private interests, and openness to revision — which we operationalize as a rubric for scoring online political discussion threads.

Idiomatic expressions, defined as multi-word units whose meaning is not compositionally derivable from the meanings of their constituent words (Nunberg et al., 1994), present a well-known challenge for natural language processing systems that rely on word-level semantics. The degree of non-compositionality varies substantially across idioms: some permit a degree of literal interpretation alongside the idiomatic reading, while others are fully opaque. Our idiom detection system targets the fully opaque end of this spectrum, training on examples drawn from curated idiom databases rather than naturally occurring corpora to avoid the confound of compositional near-misses.

The concept of informed consent in research ethics requires that participants understand the nature, purpose, risks, and voluntary nature of their participation before agreeing to take part (Beauchamp and Childress, 2001). Its application to studies involving social media data is contested: while users technically agree to platform terms of service that permit research use, it is widely acknowledged that this falls short of meaningful informed consent. We document our IRB protocol and data anonymization procedures in the supplementary materials and discuss the ethical trade-offs involved in our data collection approach.

Semantic drift, the gradual change in word meaning over time through use in new contexts (Traugott and Dasher, 2002), has attracted computational attention as large diachronic corpora have made it tractable to track distributional representations across decades or centuries. The mechanisms of drift are varied — metaphorical extension, narrowing, broadening, pejoration — and different computational methods are better suited to capturing different types. Our evaluation benchmark includes test cases spanning all four mechanisms, motivated by evidence that existing methods show uneven performance across them.

The question of whether a machine can be said to understand language has a long philosophical history, with Turing's (1950) imitation game providing the most influential early operationalization: a machine understands language if a human judge cannot distinguish its responses from those of a human in open-ended textual exchange. This behavioral criterion has been criticized from multiple directions — as too weak, too strong, or simply ill-suited to the actual capabilities we care about in practical systems — but it continues to anchor debates about the nature and evaluation of language understanding. Our work does not take a position on the philosophical question but contributes empirical data about the specific capabilities that current large language models do and do not exhibit.
